hardware: AMD Ryzen 3900X (12 cores); 2x AMD EPYC 7702 (2x64 cores)
name: Rapidgzip
baseline: GNU gzip (single-threaded deflate decoder); also compared with pigz, igzip (ISA-L), bgzip and pzstd
workload: Decompression of arbitrary gzip files (Silesia tar repeated 20x, 3.95 GiB; 4 GiB base64 data) on a Ryzen 3900X, plus scaling to 128 cores on 2x EPYC 7702.
claimed_speedup: Ryzen 3900X, 20x-silesia with existing index: 5640 MB/s (0 threads=auto) vs gzip 293 MB/s (18.8x); from scratch 2070 MB/s (6.9x); 4GiB-base64 from scratch 5060 MB/s vs gzip 250 MB/s (20.1x). README: up to 24 GB/s with index and 12 GB/s without on 128 cores; 24.3 GB/s vs 9.5 GB/s for pzstd with index. Paper abstract: 5.6 GB/s on Silesia, speedup 33 over GNU gzip, with 128 cores. README: single-core decompression close to igzip and about twice as fast as bgzip (zlib).
license: Apache-2.0 AND MIT (repo page lists both; per-file split not checked)
tradeoffs: Multi-core only wins: single-thread speed is close to igzip, not faster. Needs memory for chunk cache and a two-stage decode of unknown windows; with an index it reaches higher bandwidth. Read-only decompressor (compression is delegated to other tools). C++17, usable as header-only C++ library.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (ACM HPDC 2023, DOI 10.1145/3588195.3592992) but the paper itself was not opened (arXiv/ACM blocked here); numbers are from the README. Compiler and flags not stated on the README page. The headline gain is parallel scaling versus single-threaded gzip, not a faster single-thread inflate. Baseline is GNU gzip rather than zlib; README values for current versions are higher than the paper's table 4.
found_via: WebSearch: 'rapidgzip parallel gzip decompression paper HPDC github'

name: OpenZL
baseline: zstd -3 and xz -9 (format-aware path); zstd at equivalent settings (OpenZL LZ mode in v0.3.0)
workload: Format-aware compression of structured data (SAO file from Silesia in the launch benchmark); v0.3.0 release notes compare the OpenZL LZ configuration with zstd on an unstated dataset.
claimed_speedup: v0.3.0 release notes: OpenZL LZ decompression 3062 MB/s vs zstd 1254 MB/s (release text: 144% faster than Zstandard at equivalent settings), compression 467 vs 419 MB/s, ratio 2.73 vs 2.74. Launch benchmark (search snippet only): SAO ratio 2.06 vs zstd -3 1.31 and xz -9 1.64; compression 203 MB/s, decompression 822 MB/s vs zstd -3 115 / 890 MB/s and xz -9 3.1 / 30 MB/s.
stars_or_usage: 3.2k stars; used in production at Meta
tradeoffs: Gains need a format description or trained compressor per data type; generic input falls back to LZ-style mode. API and compressed format may change between releases (payloads from tagged releases stay decodable). Universal decoder. C11 + C++17 build, CMake/Make, CLI and Python bindings.
caveats: First-party numbers. The v0.3.0 release page does not state dataset, CPU, compiler or flags. The SAO numbers come from search-result snippets of the launch blog (engineering.fb.com, blocked here) and the whitepaper (arXiv 2510.03203, blocked), not opened. The speed win over zstd is for the new LZ mode; the SAO result trades a slightly lower decompression speed (822 vs 890 MB/s) for a much better ratio. The repo carries an optional benchmark build (OPENZL_BUILD_BENCHMARKS), not yet inspected for tier A.
found_via: WebSearch: 'OpenZL format-aware compression framework Meta paper github faster than zstd'; release notes via 'pdf site:github.com compression paper faster than zstd' query

compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.3.1 built with MOREFLAGS="-march=native"; Clang 21 on macOS, GCC 14 on Linux
hardware: Apple M2; Google Axion (Neoverse-V2, GCP C4A); AMD EPYC 9B45 (Zen 5, GCP C4D); AMD EPYC 7B13 (Zen 3, GCP C2D); SMT disabled on x86
name: ZXC
workload: Single-threaded decompression speed on the Silesia corpus (202 MB) at matched ratio tiers, measured with lzbench 2.3.1 on four machines.
claimed_speedup: Decompression speed ratio ZXC vs competitor at each tier (Apple M2 / Axion Neoverse-V2 / EPYC 9B45 / EPYC 7B13): -1 vs lz4 --fast 2.62x / 1.92x / 2.20x / 1.81x; -3 vs lz4 1.75x / 1.41x / 1.36x / 1.22x; -6 vs lz4hc -9 1.50x / 1.25x / 1.19x / 1.10x; -7 vs zstd -1 2.60x / 1.94x / 2.21x / 2.13x. Ratio also slightly smaller output in each pairing (e.g. 61.76% vs 62.15%).
stars_or_usage: 465 stars; README says merged into lzbench and TurboBench
tradeoffs: Asymmetric: slow encoder (optimal parsing) for fast decoder, aimed at write-once/read-many data. Compression speed is lower than LZ4 at the fast tier. Bindings for Rust, Python, Node.js, Go, WASM. Optional seekable archives.
caveats: Benchmarks are by the author (first party), but code, tool (lzbench), flags and CPUs are public and CI re-runs them; the README says it is merged into lzbench and TurboBench, which was not independently checked. Another repo (Vladexy88x/zxc) shows the same description and appears to be a copy. Repo is young; the speed win is largest on ARM64. WebFetch of README was summarised, then numbers re-read from the raw README.

name: LZAV
baseline: zstd -1 (decompression speed); Snappy 1.1.10; LZ4 1.9.4 for ratio
workload: Silesia corpus in-memory compression and decompression on Apple M1 3.5 GHz (Apple clang 15 arm64); also Ryzen/Intel variants in the README; zstd measured separately by the author with TurboBench on Ryzen 3700X.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1, Silesia: LZAV 5.18 627 MB/s compress, 3830 MB/s decompress, ratio 39.91%; Snappy 1.1.10 495 / 3230 MB/s, ratio 48.22%; LZ4 1.9.4 700 / 4570 MB/s, ratio 47.60%. Author's zstd 1.5.5 -1 on Ryzen 3700X (TurboBench): 436 MB/s compress, 1400 MB/s decompress, ratio 34.6%. Faster decompression than Snappy and zstd -1, smaller output than LZ4 and Snappy; but slower than LZ4 on both speeds.
tradeoffs: Scalar LZ77 only (no entropy coding), header-only, performs bounds checks on decode, portable including WebAssembly. Ratio between LZ4 and zstd -1; compression is about 30% slower than LZ4.
caveats: First party. Does NOT beat LZ4 on speed; the claim is better ratio at near-LZ4 speed and faster than Snappy. The zstd comparison mixes two different CPUs, so it is directional only. Compiler flags not stated.

hardware: Intel Core i9-7900X 3.3 GHz (10 cores, AVX512), 32 GB RAM, Linux 4.18
name: FSST (Fast Static Symbol Table)
workload: Compression of short strings (22 'dbtext' data sets, each an 8 MB file, single-threaded) with random access per string; LZ4 used in file-based mode.
claimed_speedup: PVLDB 2020 paper Table 1: compression speed FSST higher than LZ4 on most sets (e.g. genome 1,307 vs 566 MB/s, uuid 1,113 vs 632, credentials 984 vs 439) with higher compression factor (e.g. genome 3.32 vs 1.59, uuid 2.44 vs 1.55); decompression speed similar to LZ4 on average (e.g. genome 2,838 vs 1,126 MB/s, hex 1,546 vs 1,891, urls 2,296 vs 2,264). LZ4 wins on ratio for urls (2.77 vs 2.16).
tradeoffs: Strings only (symbol table of up to 8-byte symbols mapped to 1-byte codes); static table per block, random access to single strings without block decode; not a general-purpose byte-stream compressor. Best on short-string columns, ratio gain largest on machine-generated IDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (PVLDB vol 13 no 12, 2020); numbers read from the paper PDF checked into the repo (via raw.githubusercontent.com). LZ4 version is old (1.8.1) and gcc 8.3.1. Decompression is roughly on par with LZ4, not faster; the main win is ratio plus random access, and compression speed. Whether the repo ships the benchmark harness and dbtext corpus was not checked, so tier B not A.
found_via: WebSearch: 'FSST fast static symbol table string compression paper SIGMOD github cwida fsst decompression speed LZ4'

name: Kanzi (kanzi-cpp)
baseline: xz 5.8.1 -9 (encode time at similar size); also bzip2 1.0.8, bzip3, brotli, gzip
workload: Silesia tar (211,957,760 bytes) compress and decompress time and size, plus enwik8, with 16 threads, README table by the author.
claimed_speedup: Silesia, Ryzen 9 9950X: kanzi -l 6 49,472,110 bytes, 922 ms encode / 523 ms decode vs xz 5.8.1 -9 48,802,580 bytes, 43,611 ms encode / 931 ms decode; kanzi -l 5 53,863,205 bytes, 569 / 275 ms vs bzip2 -9 54,588,597 bytes, 8,223 / 3,453 ms. Derived from page data: about 47x faster encode and 1.8x faster decode than xz -9 at 1.4% larger output (thread settings: zstd and bsc rows show -T16, xz row shows none, kanzi row does not state a thread count).
tradeoffs: Modular BWT / context-mixing / transform pipeline with built-in multithreading; strong at high ratios, not at low-latency decode: zstd 1.6.0 decodes the same file in 23-26 ms vs kanzi 41-12,665 ms. Compressor, not archiver.
caveats: First-party, single run table; compiler and flags not stated; thread counts are not stated for the kanzi and xz rows, so the xz comparison may not be like for like. Not faster than zstd at decode or at equal size on the low levels (kanzi -l 1 is both bigger and slower than zstd -2). Speed win is vs xz, bzip2, bzip3, brotli at their high-ratio settings.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Blosc2 OR Kanzi compression library C++ faster than zstd benchmark github paper peer-reviewed'

name: BZip3
workload: Compression ratio and decompression time on a tarball of every released Perl 5 version, as listed in the README.
claimed_speedup: README: bzip3 -b 511 546,456,978 bytes vs xz 2,056,645,240, zstd 3,076,143,660, bzip2 3,441,163,911. Decompression time: bzip3 (parallel) 4 min 6 s, xz 4 min 40 s, zstd 3 min 51 s, bzip2 9 min 22 s (derived from page data: about 2.3x faster than bzip2, 1.14x faster than xz, but slower than zstd).
tradeoffs: BWT + context mixing + LZ/RLE; large memory use (README timings show 12-18 GB at large block sizes); the format and code are not zstd/xz compatible. Compiler-sensitive: README says clang 13 on x64 Linux reaches about 17 MiB/s compress and 23 MiB/s decompress per thread.
caveats: First party. Hardware, compiler and flags not stated near the tables. Main claim is ratio; the speed win is over bzip2 and, by a small margin, xz, while zstd decompresses faster. A GitHub issue ('Better performance claim', #2) disputes cherry-picked settings (seen as a search result, not opened).
found_via: WebSearch: 'bzip3 github kspalaiologos faster than bzip2 xz compression ratio benchmark'

hardware: Lenovo Ideapad 5 Pro, AMD Ryzen 6600HS (discussion 2351); CPU not stated in issue 986
name: ISA-L (igzip)
workload: Third-party TurboBench run on silesia.tar, Ryzen 6600HS (zlib-ng GitHub discussion 2351); separate user report decompressing a 16.4 GB gzip file (zlib-ng issue 986).
claimed_speedup: Discussion 2351 (silesia.tar): igzip level 2 598.69 MB/s compress, 1,047.07 MB/s decompress, ratio 36.1%; zlib level 9 27.79 MB/s compress, 734.94 MB/s decompress, ratio 32.2%; zlib-ng level 9 37.74 / 478.69 MB/s. Issue 986: gzip 117.76 s, pigz with zlib-ng 62.13 s, igzip 20.53 s to decompress 5.03 GB compressed to 16.4 GB (derived from page data: about 5.7x faster than gzip, 3x faster than pigz). The same discussion shows libdeflate 6 and 12 decompressing at about 1,127-1,134 MB/s, faster than igzip there.
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; used by rapidgzip, Python proposals and others
tradeoffs: Deflate-compatible only; fastest levels give a clearly worse ratio than zlib -9 (36.1% vs 32.2% in the table); hand-written x86 (NASM) and aarch64/RISC-V (gas) assembly. Linux/Windows/macOS builds via autotools or CMake; C API callable from C++.
caveats: Evidence is community-posted numbers in zlib-ng threads (author of TurboBench for 2351), not the ISA-L repo's own docs: compiler and flags are not stated, and the compared levels have different ratios. The IEEE paper 'ISA-L Igzip: Improvements to a Fast Deflate' was only seen as a search result (blocked). README page itself has no numbers. libdeflate decompresses as fast or faster in that table.

name: Recoil (parallel rANS decoding)
baseline: conventional interleaved rANS decoding and other ANS-based codecs (not zstd/lz4/zlib/brotli/xz)
workload: Parallel decoding of a single rANS bitstream on CPUs and GPUs with decoder-adaptive parallelism (ICPP 2023).
claimed_speedup: Abstract (search snippet only): decoding throughput comparable to the conventional approach, scaling massively on CPUs and GPUs, greatly outperforming various other ANS-based codecs. No numbers read.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 library (needs gcc 10+/clang 14+, CMake 3.24+, CUDA 12+). rANS entropy coder only, not a full LZ-class compressor. Docs are marked TODO; separate recoil-testscripts repo holds the experiment scripts. GPL-3.0 (LICENSE added July 2026).
caveats: Paper is peer-reviewed (ICPP 2023, DOI 10.1145/3605573.3605588) but arXiv (2306.12141) and the ACM page are blocked here and no numbers were seen, so tier C for now; a verifier with paper access could raise it to B. Baseline is other ANS codecs, off the zlib/zstd/lz4/brotli/xz list. GPL means copyable only under GPL terms.

name: zlib-rs
workload: inflate (decompression) and deflate across levels, comparing API-compatible zlib implementations (project blog).
claimed_speedup: Search snippets of the project blog posts: zlib-rs 'the fastest API-compatible zlib implementation for decompression', beating zlib-ng 'by a fair margin' and Chromium's zlib; compression faster in the most important cases but on par with zlib-ng at the highest level and 'much worse' at the lowest level. No numbers read. The repo README itself says 'generally on-par with zlib-ng'.
tradeoffs: Memory-safe Rust; usable from C++ through the libz-rs-sys C API (cdylib). Based on zlib and zlib-ng code. Needs a Rust toolchain; fastest results need non-default RUSTFLAGS. Weak at the lowest compression levels.
caveats: Blog posts (trifectatech.org) are blocked here, so the claims are snippet-only and no CPU or numbers were seen. Its own README claims parity with zlib-ng, not a clear win. Other-language entry whose claim is against a C incumbent (zlib-ng, which is already catalogued); consider folding into the zlib-ng entry.

hardware: AWS Graviton3 c7g.2xlarge; also Sapphire Rapids c7i.2xlarge
name: Glyd
workload: 8.7 GB real-data corpus (logs, JSON events, SQL dumps, Parquet), one core and eight cores, plus record-mode and storage tests.
claimed_speedup: One core on AWS Graviton3: Glyd default ratio 2.82, 332 MB/s compress, 3,309 MB/s decompress vs LZ4 ratio 2.72, 504 / 1,394 MB/s and zstd -3 ratio 3.86, 313 / 1,425 MB/s; Glyd --max ratio 3.98, 233 / 1,571 MB/s. Eight cores: Glyd default 22,707 MB/s decompress vs zstd -3 -T8 1,422 MB/s and LZ4 1,392 MB/s. README summary: reads 3-7x faster than zstd on a server and writes at 0.77x zstd -3 speed.
license: BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0 (codec); BUSL-1.1 (glyd-store and GPU parts)
tradeoffs: Codec is dual-licensed but the store and GPU components are under Business Source License 1.1 (commercial use needs a license). Output decodes in parallel, so multicore reads are far faster than zstd/LZ4 frames that decode on one thread. Compresses slower than LZ4 and zstd -3 at the same levels; record mode costs 2-2.7x the CPU of zstd. Rust crate with C ABI callable from C++.
caveats: First party, very young repo with sweeping claims (title says world's fastest-decoding). README itself says one-core reads on Sapphire Rapids are slower than zstd (0.79-0.97x for --max) and small objects favour zstd. The 22.7 GB/s figure compares 8-thread Glyd with single-thread-decoded zstd/LZ4 frames, not like for like. Compiler/flags not confirmed; reproduce scripts exist in repo (scripts/bench_aws_suite.sh) and a full results file is docs/benchmarks/suite-2026-09-21.md, neither opened.
